title: The Currency Gap Every Australian Exporter Feels Between the Quote and the Payment
linkedin:
An exporter can price a deal perfectly and still watch the margin disappear before the money lands.

Not because anything went wrong operationally. Because of what happens to the exchange rate between the day a price is quoted and the day the payment actually converts into Australian dollars.

That gap is longer than most owners picture. Quote at the start of a production run, ship eight weeks later, get paid on 60 or 90 day terms, and the currency exposure window can stretch past four months. A lot can move in that time, and none of it shows up until the bank statement lands.

The pattern we see across exporters: currency risk gets treated as a treasury issue, separate from pricing, checked occasionally rather than managed as policy. Whoever is looking at the bank account that week ends up making the call under time pressure, which is rarely when the best decision gets made.

The businesses that protect their margin do it differently. They build an exchange rate buffer into the quote itself, track exposure contract by contract rather than as one lump balance sheet figure, and use tools like forward contracts consistently rather than only when the rate happens to look favourable.

None of this requires predicting where the dollar goes. It requires a policy that protects the business regardless of which way it moves.

Here's one we see a lot with exporters: the deal was priced properly, the shipment went out fine, and the margin still came in thinner than expected.

The culprit is usually the exchange rate. Whatever rate was sitting there on quote day is not the rate that applies by the time payment actually lands and converts, sometimes months later. A small move against a tight margin is the difference between a good contract and a forgettable one.

If you're exporting, when did you last actually check how long the gap is between quoting a job and the payment landing? For a lot of businesses it's longer than they'd guess.

A note for local business owners who sell into overseas markets, whether that's a manufacturer shipping product, a services firm invoicing an international client, or anyone getting paid in a currency other than Australian dollars.

The margin on a deal is usually calculated using the exchange rate on the day a price is quoted. But that is not the rate that actually applies. The real number is set on the day the payment lands and gets converted back into Australian dollars, and that can be weeks or even months after the quote was given. In that gap, the exchange rate can move enough to turn a solid margin into a thin one, or the other way around, without anything about the work itself changing.

The businesses that handle this well do not leave it to chance. They build a buffer into their pricing, keep track of how exposed each contract or shipment is, and have a consistent policy for locking in exchange rates ahead of time rather than deciding on the fly when the rate happens to look good.

If your business gets paid in a foreign currency and you have never actually mapped out how long that exposure window is, this is worth ten minutes of your time. Read the full piece on the ProfitPulse blog.
